body.text: COP may have reached its use-by date, but it's hard to imagine a replacement
Paul Keating's brutal takedowns of opponents birthed one of the great political insults of our time: the "low-altitude flyer".
It's glorious. And the reason it cuts to the quick is because politicians can have fragile egos. Everyone fancies themselves touching the ionosphere in a thundering starship of greatness.
Nobody wants to be cast as the plodder hugging the ground in a flatulent crop-duster.
But the last few days have seen swarms of the latter taking flight.
The cause of their epicaricacy was Chris Bowen, the climate minister whose Icarian effort to land a planetary climate agreement flamed out this week.
If people remember anything about this year's UN climate summit in Türkiye it will surely be that image of Bowen, slouched despondent in his seat as President of Negotiations.
Framed by glum-looking advisors, a study in grimness. Wings singed.
Like a fighter shut down by the referee. Punched out.
It's exactly what Bowen's critics lusted for: confirmation that his vanity project of leading a COP had led to international humiliation and diplomatic embarrassment.

He's been copping it from both ends. The anti-climate action brigade fumed that the money spent on Australia's co-hosting efforts was wasted, while the pro-climate action squad blamed the Albanese government's ongoing fossil fuel support for undermining Bowen's "moral authority" on the global stage.
Which is something the minister this week rejected, pointing out that Australia is both an exporter of fossil fuels and shifting rapidly to a renewables-dominated grid.
"Every country in the world is one of two things: a fossil fuel exporter or a fossil fuel importer. We're all part of the supply chain," he told 7.30 on Wednesday.
"There's no more onus on one particular part or the other. We're in it together. We've all got to reduce emissions. We've all got to transition away from fossil fuels."
'Everyone's shitty'
After attending five climate summits, Bowen told this columnist they always start with various parties "wide apart" on how far to progress.
His greatest surprise this year was the degree to which relationships on the global stage have become more "personal" and "toxic".
The climate change and energy minister said he spent much of the year working out who might block the process.
The Chinese, he said, "were great, constructive, engaged" and prepared to back his global push for an electrification target. India likewise.
The problems emerged between Saudi Arabia and the Europeans. "Everyone's shitty. Saudi Arabia versus Europe. It was visceral."
"This time they didn't care whether they got a deal," he said, adding that it took two days to get the two sides to meet. With a four-day process "you can't work like this".
Splitting the COP was the question of whether to include language in a declaration reiterating the 2023 COP statement in support of TAFF or "transition away from fossil fuels".
Held in Dubai that year, the 2023 meeting agreed on TAFF because the Americans under Joe Biden and John Kerry had helped push the Saudis, he suggested.
That dynamic is absent in the Trump era.
COPs — with their near-absurd consensus structure — have long had varying degrees of success.

The 2015 Paris edition saw Tony Abbott sign up Australia to limiting global warming to between 1.5 degrees Celsius and 2 degrees Celsius, with the world to attain a balance between climate pollution and abatement by 2050.
Six years later in Glasgow, when Scott Morrison led Australia's delegation, the conference agreed to bring 90 per cent of global GDP into net zero, Australia included.
That history hints at many things. But above all is the reality that most COPs are incremental at best.
When the cumbersome mechanism manages to ratchet forward it's almost a miracle, given the fact that more than 190 countries can individually kill any agreement.

COPs are akin to the Australian parliament only passing legislation on condition that "Barnaby Joyce agreed to it, and the Greens, and all of us in between, and every single MP had a power of veto", Bowen said in the 7.30 interview.
"I'm not sure we'd get much legislation through the House of Representatives, but that's how COP works."
The Republican elephant in the room
The earlier summits in both Paris and Glasgow were examples of Australia using its diplomacy and statecraft to help shape major initiatives on the world stage.
Bowen has been an enthusiastic and determined carrier of that tradition and pressed hard to host this year's meeting in Adelaide, before settling for co-hosting duties with Türkiye.
But blaming him for this year's failure is simplistic, given the realpolitik of today's geopolitical circumstances.
Had he succeeded, it's doubtful some of those same critics would have lauded him.
"Without America there and a Democratic president there it's not going to change," Bowen told this columnist.
That's unlikely to change at next year's meeting in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, nor the COP in 2028, given it will likely pre-date the next US presidential election.
By which time there will have been almost half a decade of failure, he says.
Which raises a key question. Has the annual UN climate summit — with all its excesses — at last reached its use-by date?
"It may well have."
What might stand in its place is harder to imagine.
Perhaps a new grouping or structure that accepts that some countries like Saudi Arabia are better off left outside the tent. Countries that are committed can then build momentum.
Either way, smashing up Bowen for his role and ambition to host a COP — a goal that was taken to the 2022 election and endorsed by voters again in 2025 — is dishonest tosh.
The stuff of low-altitude flyers.
"I wouldn't do it again, but I don't regret trying. Australia has to play its role in these things," he concludes.
Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.
